reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / hepatology reference literature
clinicalPearls: A self-limiting triad of haemolytic anaemia, transient hyperlipidaemia and jaundice occurring after heavy alcohol use, usually on a background of fatty liver or alcoholic hepatitis
Should be suspected when jaundice and anaemia in an alcohol-dependent patient are accompanied by an unexpectedly high lipid profile
The haemolysis is Coombs-negative, distinguishing it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Abdominal pain and tender hepatomegaly are common, mimicking other acute hepatobiliary emergencies
Bilirubin is disproportionately elevated relative to the degree of hepatocellular injury because of the haemolytic contribution
The hyperlipidaemia and haemolysis typically resolve within weeks of alcohol cessation and supportive care
Recognition avoids unnecessary invasive haemolysis and biliary work-up, as the condition remits with abstinence
reference.pathophysiology: Zieve syndrome develops in the setting of alcohol-related liver injury, where transient hyperlipidaemia and abnormal red-cell membrane lipid composition render erythrocytes fragile and prone to haemolysis. Pyruvate-kinase instability and altered red-cell membrane cholesterol and phospholipid content, together with the effects of acute alcohol excess, are thought to shorten red-cell survival. The combination of haemolysis-driven unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and coexisting cholestatic liver injury produces marked jaundice, while the associated hyperlipidaemia is characteristically transient and resolves with abstinence.
additionalDifferentials: Spur-cell haemolytic anaemia of advanced liver disease
Haemolysis from another cause such as G6PD deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film assessing for haemolysis
Reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, expected to be negative
Fasting lipid profile demonstrating transient hyperlipidaemia
Liver function tests and abdominal ultrasound to characterise the liver and exclude obstruction
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring urgent transfusion
Features of decompensated alcoholic hepatitis or liver failure
Signs of biliary obstruction or cholangitis needing intervention
Very high triglycerides with associated pancreatitis
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is self-limiting and carries a good prognosis with alcohol cessation and supportive care, though the underlying alcohol-related liver disease governs the longer-term outlook.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the haemolysis as autoimmune and starting inappropriate immunosuppression
Attributing all the jaundice to hepatocellular disease and missing the haemolytic contribution
Undertaking extensive haemolysis or biliary investigations before considering the diagnosis
Overlooking the transient hyperlipidaemia, a key clue to the syndrome
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Hepatology reference literature on alcohol-related haemolysis
management: Alcohol cessation is the definitive treatment, as the haemolysis and hyperlipidaemia resolve with abstinence
Provide supportive care with transfusion for severe symptomatic anaemia and management of the underlying alcoholic liver disease
Give nutritional repletion with thiamine, folate and other B vitamins, and manage or prevent alcohol withdrawal
Avoid unnecessary immunosuppression, recognising the Coombs-negative haemolysis is not autoimmune, and confirm with a negative direct antiglobulin test
Monitor the haemolytic markers (reticulocytes, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin) and the lipid profile as they normalise
Refer to alcohol-dependence and hepatology services for relapse prevention and assessment of liver disease
Escalate for severe anaemia or decompensating liver disease
